Stadium guide How each stadium changes the mix of hits (Seasons 2 to 5, 184 games)

Compared with the league, as a multiplier (1.0 = average). Small samples are pulled toward 1.0. The box scores show no stadium effect on how often a batter gets a hit, and no team or player does better or worse in a particular stadium than their ratings say, so the picks come from these hit-type shifts and each team's mix of power and speed. Wall distances are a fan's timing estimates (rough). They feed the home run robbery rule in the sim: a fast outfield reaches the wall in time, more easily in a small park, and a center fielder with chemistry to both corners (buddy jump) catches many more. The box scores are too coarse to confirm the size of that effect (no measurable change in home runs allowed by outfield speed), so it is set small.

What matters most

Which stats to prioritize

Rounds 1 to the "best available" limit weigh the stat mix first, then whether the player will still be there at that coach's next pick, then chemistry. After that, chemistry leads. The Plan-ahead, Scarcity and Past-draft sliders shape the computer coaches; for your own picks only Plan-ahead and Positional fit apply, because the availability simulation already reflects the other two. Sliders scale those defaults: 0 ignores a factor and 3× triples it. "All teams" sets the baseline for everyone and clears that slider's overrides. Picking a team edits only that coach. Your team's settings drive your recommendations. OBP is the same as batting average in this league: the box scores show essentially no walks.

Unpredictability by team 0 always takes the model's top choice · 1.5 is wild

Set a drafter you know well: low for someone who takes the obvious best player, high for someone who falls in love with sleepers. Moving the all-teams slider resets every team to that value. Changes apply to the next computer pick and the availability odds.

How the model works

Player projections. Each player's hit rates (1B, 2B, 3B, HR per at-bat) come from the Career Stats sheet, blended toward what their Game Stats ratings predict when the sample is small (about 120 at-bats of weight on the ratings). Pitchers work the same way with hits allowed and runs per 9, with about 30 innings of weight on the ratings; unproven pitchers start slightly worse than league average. Stamina sets how many innings a pitcher can cover.

Recommendations. A pick's value is how much it raises your team's projected runs per game once lineup, pitching staff, chemistry and the outfield rule are rebuilt with them in it. Empty slots are filled with replacement-level players, so value is measured against what you could get late. "Avail. next" is the share of 60 quick simulations of the other teams' picks in which the player is still there at your next turn.

How the other teams draft. Through round 4 (adjustable above) they start from one shared ranking of player value and ONM, but chemistry still counts a lot: a player who links to the roster they have, or can still be tied in by someone left on the board, gets a big boost, and a player with no link now and no way to get one is marked down. So the best available is the best one they can connect (Royals would not take King Boo first with no plan to link him; if a team does, its next picks go to connecting him). From round 5 on they take the player with the most chemistry links to the players they already have, using player value to break ties. Each team's unpredictability setting adds randomness to both; set it per team in Setup. With the Mii toggle on, Miis are left off the best-available board, and in chemistry rounds a Mii is only considered when it has good chemistry with the roster, scored on chemistry alone. Captain rules apply in every round. Your own recommendations always weigh overall team fit, so you can see where the chemistry drafters leave value behind.

Rules enforced. The captain rule (once the teams without a captain equal the captains left, those teams must take one, and teams that already have a captain cannot take another), the requirement for a rostered captain, and CF chemistry with both corner outfielders. Chemistry cells marked yellow in the sheet depend on color: a Mii only has chemistry with the same color of that character (Blue Mii with Blue Toad, not Purple Toad). Teams with fewer than 9 picks are filled from the best undrafted players before the season sim.

Priorities. Each pick is scored on three things: a stat mix (team gain, runs contributed, OBP, power, pitching, sexy plays, ONM and speed, each with its own slider, with team gain the lightest by default), availability (how likely the player is gone before that coach's next pick, which raises the value of players who will not last), and chemistry with the current roster. The defaults favor stats, then availability, then chemistry through the best-available rounds, and chemistry after. The Draft priorities sliders scale each one, per coach. No Miis are suggested or drafted by computer teams before the round set in Draft settings.

Draft theory from past drafts. Seasons 1 to 5 are loaded (Season 5 Golden Blocks left out, since they randomized). Each player has an average pick, converted to a 10-team league with recent seasons counted more, and computer coaches are pulled toward a player once the draft reaches the slot where he usually goes, and away from taking him much earlier. Teams also take a good player who is not the best one left when he is scarce and other teams need him: a player's demand is how many other teams already own a chemistry partner for him (Boo in round 2 because several teams had Kameks, or a Mii whose color many teams need). Teams also draft for chemistry they cannot use yet: a player with no link to the roster today counts for more when someone still on the board would connect him (Hammer Bro, then Boo, then Kamek, or a green Dry Bones now and a green Mii later). The Past-draft tendencies, Scarcity and Plan-ahead chemistry sliders control these, per coach. In the test drafts these factors raised the match to real draft history from about 0.70 to about 0.91 (correlation of average pick). Miis have gone as early as round 2 in the past (JT in Season 2), but the no-Miis-before-round-4 rule is kept because you asked for it.

Roster theory. Players are placed by what they do well, not just value: sexy plays and glove go to shortstop and second base, speed goes to the outfield, and pitchers are chosen by pitching, stamina and rating. Slow players such as Kritters and King Boo are steered away from the outfield unless chemistry forces it, and the draft logic includes a positional fit term (slider under the stats) so a team looks for speed in the outfield and sexy plays up the middle. The batting order goes for items first: when the batter behind a hitter has chemistry with him, he can use an item when the ball is hit (9th hitter to 1st counts). The Rosters tab counts items for every team, marks each hitter who has one, and can re-order your starters for items, for a balance, or the classic way with the best hitters at 3 and 4. In the game sim each item adds a small hit bonus (1.0% hit odds by default; the slider on the Rosters tab sets it, and 0 turns it off). That value is a judgment call: the box scores do not record batting orders, so item use cannot be measured directly. Only starters bat, field or pitch. Pitching follows the league rule that the captain comes in right after the first pitcher, so the staff is opener, captain, then the rest; your box scores back this up (the second pitcher was a captain in 143 of 147 two-pitcher games).

What the box scores show. Seasons 2 to 5 (184 games): teams score 6.8 runs a game (5.9 in Season 4, 7.0 in Season 5), home teams win exactly 50%, and 23% of games go past 7 innings. Hitters bat .463 with no walks, so on-base is the same as batting average, and 4.5% of at-bats are home runs. Exactly nine players bat for each team in a game, so bench depth never plays. The model's team rating tracks real results (correlation 0.59 over 30 team-seasons, and each rating run is worth about 1.2 actual runs, so the scale is right). Chemistry points added about 0.16 runs a game each to runs scored, with no effect on runs allowed; that is roughly 2 standard errors from zero and larger than the old weight, so the chemistry weight went from 0.06 to 0.10 instead of all the way up. A direct test found no change in a hitter's own hit rate from having more chemistry partners in the lineup, which points to items as the channel. Chemistry does produce defense: buddy catches and throws per player-game rise from 0.007 with no chemistry partners to 0.24 with four or more. Ballpark differences (Luigi Mansion 5.3 runs, Yoshi Park 7.5) rest on 16 to 25 games each, so they are treated as noise. All of these are small samples, so treat them as direction, not proof.

Outfield and home runs. The center fielder has to have chemistry with both corner outfielders, and the starting pitcher cannot also be one of the three, so the lineup and the positions are built around a valid trio. In the game sim a home run can be caught at the wall. The chance rises with outfield speed (center fielder weighted most) and with a short wall, and it is much higher when the buddy-jump chemistry rule is met. On average about 5% of home runs are caught, from about 2% for a slow outfield to about 7% for a fast one.

Games. Plate appearances are simulated batter versus pitcher using those rates, with fielding, errors, double plays and base running. The league-wide scoring level is tuned to your sheet's history (about 6.5 runs per team per 7 innings).
